Newly settled spat of the Northern bay mussel (Mytilus trossulus) emerge from the egg capsule with a shell height of approximately 0.011 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.011 centimeters], a dimension measured from the umbo to the ventral margin. At this initial stage, the corresponding dry tissue weight is on the order of 0.0000007 grams , reflecting the minute size of the newly hatched, non-feeding larva. In laboratory trials maintained at a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the interval from egg fertilization to this hatching event, or age at birth, was recorded as just 1.75 days [ab = 1.75 days], indicating a rapid early development typical of many marine bivalves. Following eclosion, the veliger larva enters a brief planktotrophic phase, during which it feeds on phytoplankton and grows steadily. The time elapsed from hatching to the point of larval metamorphosis, when the veliger settles and undergoes its morphological transformation into a post-larval juvenile, was observed to be 22 days from hatching  under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C].

Upon achieving metamorphic competence and completing the larval-juvenile transition, the recently metamorphosed spat already weighs about 0.00001035 grams  dry tissue mass. This value is consistent with an isometric scaling relationship based on the increase in shell height from the 0.011 centimeters [Lb = 0.011 centimeters] at birth to a height of 0.027 centimeters  at the point of settlement. The shell height at metamorphosis itself, measured from the umbo to the ventral margin, is thus 0.027 centimeters . This allometric shift in body plan, marked by velum loss and the development of functional gills, allows the juvenile to transition from a pelagic to a benthic lifestyle. Field surveys in protected intertidal habitats indicate that the period of rapid juvenile growth following settlement is energetically demanding, with individuals needing to accumulate sufficient somatic tissue before the onset of gametogenesis.

Sexual maturation, or puberty, in Mytilus trossulus is attained when individuals reach a shell height of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters] as measured from the umbo to the ventral margin. At this size threshold, the dry tissue weight of a maturing individual has grown to 0.75 grams . In a controlled environment held at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the time elapsed since birth to the attainment of this pubertal stage was recorded as 365 days [tp = 365 days]. This duration matches values reported for the congener Mytilus edulis and appears reasonable for Mytilus trossulus under similar thermal regimes. The onset of reproductive activity is thus a gradual process, dependent on both somatic growth and seasonal cues. Once reproductively mature, individuals enter a spawning season where they release gametes into the water column, with fertilization occurring externally. The reproductive output of a single, maximally fecund individual under these conditions is substantial.

During the peak spawning period at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a single gravid individual can release up to 16,400 oocytes per day [Ri = up to 16,400 oocytes per day], representing the maximum recorded daily reproductive rate for this species. This prodigious gamete output reflects the high fecundity typical of broadcast-spawning bivalves, which must compensate for substantial egg mortality in the plankton. The adult body size that supports this level of reproductive investment is considerable. The ultimate shell height, representing the maximum size attained by a fully grown adult, reaches 7.08 centimeters [Li = 7.08 centimeters] from the umbo to the ventral margin. Correspondingly, the ultimate dry tissue weight of a fully grown individual, or its maximum adult dry mass, is 3.4 grams . This large size is accompanied by a substantial investment in gonadal tissue each season.

The complete lifespan of Mytilus trossulus, from the moment of hatching to natural senescence, has been documented as 1260 days [am = 1260 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This maximum recorded longevity, equivalent to roughly three and a half years, is typical for a relatively fast-growing bivalve of this size class from temperate waters. The species thus completes its entire life history from a minute, yolk-dependent larva to a reproductively mature adult that attains sexual maturity around 365 days after birth [tp = around 365 days after birth] within a compressed ti at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]meframe. Under these controlled thermal conditions, a veliger larva settles 22 days after hatching , and the initial values of 0.0000007 grams  dry weight at birth and 0.011 centimeters [Lb = 0.011 centimeters] shell height mark the start of a developmental trajectory that culminates in a substantial adult size at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The annual reproductive cycle ensures that local populations can rebound quickly following disturbance, with the timing of spawning closely linked to spring phytoplankton blooms that provide abundant food for the newly hatched planktotrophic larvae.
